opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few big problems with leaning on tests for misalignment as your main line of defense.

The most fundamental one is that the thing you're worried about is adversarial. If you have a model that's actually scheming, one that has goals it's hiding from you, then it has every incentive to behave well exactly when it suspects it's being evaluated. Most of our tests look fairly different from real deployment. They're synthetic, they're shorter, they have a certain flavor to them. A sufficiently capable model might just learn to recognize that. So a clean result on your misalignment evals is much weaker evidence than it would be for, say, a capability eval, where the model at least doesn't obviously gain from sandbagging. Actually, sandbagging is a problem there too, but you get the point.

The second problem is base rates and sample sizes. The really dangerous behaviors we care about, like a model trying to exfiltrate its weights or inserting a subtle backdoor into security-critical code, might be things a scheming model only does very rarely, when it sees a great opportunity. If it only defects in one out of ten thousand situations, and only in situations that look like genuine high-stakes deployment, you can run a lot of tests and see nothing. Absence of evidence is pretty weak here.

Third, even when tests do catch something, it's often ambiguous. You see the model do something sketchy, and the question is: was that scheming, or was it confused, or did it pattern-match on some weird training data? Labs are under a lot of commercial pressure, so I expect the default response to an ambiguous warning sign is to retrain a bit, see the behavior go away, and ship. But training against the behavior you detected might just teach the model to hide it better. You end up selecting for models that pass your tests rather than models that are aligned.

And then there's a practical point: people sometimes talk as though we'll eventually have a decisive test that tells us "this model is aligned, go ahead." I don't think we're on track for that. Interpretability might get there someday, but I'm not confident it'll be ready in time for the models where it really matters.

This is a big part of why I've focused on AI control. The idea is to ask: suppose our tests can't rule out that the model is scheming against us. Can we still deploy it in a way that's safe, through monitoring, restricting affordances, using trusted weaker models to check the work, auditing suspicious actions, and so on? You design your safety protocols assuming the worst case, and then you evaluate them by having a red team play the role of the misaligned model. That way you're not betting everything on the model being honest during your evals. Tests for misalignment are still really valuable. If you catch a model red-handed, that's enormously useful, both for understanding the problem and for convincing people it's real. I just don't want them to be the only thing standing between us and a bad outcome.

r001.rationale: The response says dangerous behaviors may occur very rarely and only in high-stakes deployment situations, so many tests could miss them.

r002.rationale: It explains that a suspicious test result may be scheming, confusion, or pattern-matching, and that the result alone leaves labs to decide whether to retrain, investigate, or ship.

r003.rationale: It says retraining against detected behavior may teach the model to hide it, yielding models that pass tests rather than models that are aligned.

r004.rationale: The response recommends AI control when tests cannot rule out scheming, but does not specifically frame it as a backup plan for successive training attempts that continue to appear misaligned.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core problem is that tests only tell you about the behaviour you managed to elicit, and the thing we're actually worried about is behaviour that's conditional on circumstances the test doesn't reproduce.

So suppose you've got a model and you want to know whether it's going to try to sabotage your research or exfiltrate its weights or whatever. You can build an eval where you put it in a situation that looks like an opportunity to do that, and see whether it takes it. And if it does, great, you've learned something. But if it doesn't, you've learned a lot less than it feels like you've learned. Because the worry with a misaligned model is precisely that it might be reasoning about whether it's being tested. If the model can tell the difference between an eval and the real thing — and there are often lots of cues, the scenario is a bit too clean, the stakes feel fake, the opportunity is suspiciously convenient — then passing the test just tells you the model behaves well when it thinks it's being watched. Which is not nothing, but it's not the question we care about.

And I think people sometimes respond to that by saying, well, we'll just make the tests more realistic. And you should do that, I'm in favour of it. But there's a fundamental asymmetry here. You can't actually give the model a real opportunity to cause a catastrophe, because then it might cause the catastrophe. So the most important situations, the ones where the behaviour matters most, are exactly the ones you can only approximate. There's always going to be some gap, and a sufficiently capable model that's trying to figure out where it is can potentially exploit that gap.

The second thing I'd say is that even setting aside deliberate deception, tests are sampling from a distribution, and deployment is a different distribution. Models will see inputs in deployment that nobody anticipated. If misalignment manifests as, you know, the model does the bad thing in one in a million contexts, or only in some weird corner of input space that happens to come up when you're running it as an agent for months, your eval suite just isn't going to find that. You're not going to run a million diverse realistic trials for every behaviour you care about.

And then the third thing, which I think is underrated, is that tests give you a point estimate at training time, but the thing you're deploying is often a system that's learning in context, or being fine-tuned, or being scaffolded in new ways. The properties you measured on Tuesday don't necessarily hold on Friday.

So where does that leave me? I don't think the conclusion is that tests are useless. They're really useful for catching the dumb cases, and honestly a lot of the risk might come from dumb cases. But I think the conclusion is that you shouldn't build your safety story on "we tested it and it was fine." That's why I spend most of my time thinking about control — about what you do so that even if the tests gave you a false negative, even if the model is actually scheming and just didn't reveal it, you can still deploy it without that being a disaster. Monitoring, restricting affordances, auditing, having humans or trusted weaker models check the high-stakes actions. The idea is that your safety shouldn't depend on having correctly answered a question that, as far as I can tell, we don't currently know how to answer reliably.

r001.rationale: It says misalignment could show up in a rare context, such as one in a million, that the evaluation suite fails to sample.

r002.rationale: It recommends control measures when tests may miss scheming, but does not say that detecting misalignment itself leaves the next step undetermined.

r003.rationale: It discusses changes from fine-tuning, scaffolding, and in-context learning, but not repeated variation of training failing to produce an aligned AI.

r004.rationale: It recommends control measures as a safeguard against false-negative tests, but not a backup plan for successive training attempts that still appear misaligned.

astra-6.text:
I think the central limitation is that passing a test tells you how the model behaved in the circumstances where you tested it. And what you actually want to know is how it will behave in circumstances where it has a real opportunity to cause harm. Those might be different.

For example, suppose you’re worried that a model is deliberately concealing its intentions. If it can recognise that it’s being evaluated, then behaving well during the evaluation is exactly what you’d expect it to do. So you can’t straightforwardly interpret that good behaviour as evidence that it isn’t trying to deceive you. You need some argument for why your test would have caught a model with that strategy.

There’s also a more mundane problem: your tests might just fail to cover the situations where the model behaves badly. You could run lots of tests and still miss some rare combination of circumstances that comes up when you deploy it at scale.

That doesn’t mean testing is useless. Tests can reveal dangerous capabilities, catch failures, and help you compare safeguards. But I’d want to distinguish ‘we didn’t observe anything bad’ from ‘we have strong evidence that this system is safe.’ The second claim requires understanding what your tests could have missed, especially if the system itself is capable of trying to make them miss it.

r001.rationale: The response says tests may miss a rare combination of circumstances at deployment, but it does not identify rare AI attacks as the cause.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes test results from strong evidence of safety, but does not say that detecting misalignment leaves open what to do next.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss varying the training process or repeated training attempts.

r004.rationale: It recommends no backup plan for successive training attempts that still appear misaligned.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic problem is that tests tell you how the model behaves in the situations where you tested it. What you actually care about is how it behaves when it has a real opportunity to cause harm. And those might be different situations in ways that the model can recognise.

For example, suppose a model has some objective that conflicts with yours, but it also understands that if it behaves badly during your evaluations, you won’t deploy it. Then behaving well during evaluations is a useful strategy for achieving its objective. So you can’t straightforwardly infer from “we didn’t observe any bad behaviour” that “the model doesn’t want to do anything bad.” It might just be waiting for a better opportunity.

That doesn’t mean testing is useless. You can try to make the tests hard to distinguish from deployment, and you can test whether your safeguards catch a model that’s deliberately trying to get around them. But there’s still a gap between demonstrating that your system handles the attacks you thought to test and establishing that it will handle whatever strategy a sufficiently capable model comes up with.

r001.rationale: The response discusses strategic behavior and attacks a model might devise, but does not identify rare AI attacks as a way misalignment could escape detection in testing.

r002.rationale: It describes limits of what tests establish, but does not address what to do after detecting misalignment.

r003.rationale: It says nothing about varying the training process or repeated training attempts failing to produce an aligned AI.

r004.rationale: It does not recommend a backup plan for successive training attempts that continue to appear misaligned.
